data.text:
I searched each claim.

**Claim 0: Mount Fuji is a stratovolcano 3,776 meters tall. Supported as written.**
- NASA Earth Observatory: "The 3,776-meter-high (12,388 feet) Mount Fuji Volcano ... is one of the world's classic examples of a stratovolcano." URL: https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/39099/mount-fuji-japan
- UNESCO World Heritage nomination: a stratovolcano rising to an altitude of 3,776 m. URL: https://whc.unesco.org/en/documents/172852

**Claim 1: stratovolcanoes are built of alternating layers of lava flows and ash. Supported as written (a simplification).**
- USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory: composite volcanoes (stratovolcanoes) are steep-sided cones built of alternating layers of lava flows, ash and other debris; each eruption adds material to the slopes. URL: https://webarchive.library.unt.edu/eot2008/20090509054955/http://vulcan.wr.usgs.gov/Glossary/StratoVolcano/description_composite_volcano.html
- NPS, Composite volcanoes: notes the layers are often not orderly. URL: https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/composite-volcanoes.htm

**Claim 2: gas dissolved in magma expands as it rises and drives explosive eruptions. Supported as written.**
- USGS Soda Bottle Volcano activity: the expanding gas provides the energy that blasts magma to the surface in an explosive eruption; bubbles exsolve as pressure drops. URL: https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/19/downloads/Chapter_1/Activities/SodaBottle_volcano.pdf
- USGS, Volcanic gases on the Island of Hawaii: as magma rises, pressure decreases and gas is released. URL: https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70168947
